units.title: Japanese sounds and hiragana

lessons.title: 1. Hiragana, katakana and kanji
lessons.subtitle: The three writing systems · Where each is used · Romaji

explanations.title: Three kinds of characters
explanations.body: Japanese is written with three kinds of characters: hiragana, katakana and kanji. All three can appear in one sentence. Hiragana and katakana, like an alphabet, stand for sounds. Kanji, or Chinese characters, stand for meanings as well as sounds.

examples.text: テレビを 見ます。
examples.translation: Terebi o mimasu. — I watch television.

explanations.title: What each one is used for
explanations.body: In 「テレビを 見ます」, テレビ is katakana, 見 is kanji, and を and ます are hiragana.

rows: Verb and adjective endings, function words such as particles, and native Japanese words not covered by kanji
Nouns and the stems of verbs and adjectives; they carry meaning

explanations.title: Rōmaji
explanations.body: There is a fourth system, rōmaji (Roman letters). It is used for station names, signs and so on. In this course rōmaji appears under the Japanese as a help; do not lean on it, because the aim is to read the real characters. The romaji here follows the Genki books: a long vowel is written double (sensee, ookii), and the particles は, へ and を are spelled by sound (wa, e, o).

explanations.title: Forty-six basic hiragana
explanations.body: There are forty-six basic hiragana syllables. Once you can read this chart you can write every Japanese sound. Tap a kana to hear it. The first five rows are here; the rest are in the next lesson.

explanations.title: The vowels and the k, s, t, n rows
explanations.body: A to o are the five vowels. Each row after that pairs one consonant with the five vowels.

tables.title: Hiragana, first five rows: romaji
tables.note: し, ち and つ are romanized shi, chi and tsu so that they look like their English sound. The consonant in the same column is not written; the romaji shows how it is said.

explanations.title: Five vowels
explanations.body: The five vowels are short and clear, always read the same: a as in father, i as in see, u as in put (lips not rounded), e as in met, o as in more.

explanations.title: The rest of the chart
explanations.body: Here are the last rows. You now have all forty-six basic hiragana, counting ん.

tables.title: Hiragana, last five rows: romaji
tables.note: ふ is romanized fu. を is also romanized wo, but it is pronounced o. ん is a syllable by itself, written n.

explanations.title: ん
explanations.body: ん is the only hiragana that is a consonant alone. It counts as a full syllable in length, so ほん is two beats.

explanations.title: Two particles written with letters that sound different
explanations.body: は is pronounced wa when it is the topic particle, and を is pronounced o. Both are always written this way when they are particles; you will meet them in Lesson 1. All other wa sounds are written わ.

explanations.title: Twenty-three more sounds
explanations.body: You can write 23 more sounds with diacritical marks. A pair of short diagonal strokes (dakuten) turns the voiceless consonants k, s, t and h into the voiced g, z, d and b. A small circle (handakuten) turns h into p.

explanations.title: A small や, ゆ or よ
explanations.body: A small や, ゆ or よ written after a kana from the second column (the i-vowel hiragana, except い) transcribes a contracted sound. The contracted sound is a single syllable: きゃ is one beat, kya, not ki-ya.

tables.title: Contracted sounds: romaji
tables.note: Compare ひや (hi-ya, two syllables) with ひゃ (hya, one syllable). The small kana is what makes the difference.

lessons.title: 6. Double consonants and the small っ
lessons.subtitle: かった and かた · さっか · ざっし · さんねん

explanations.title: The small っ
explanations.body: Another small letter, っ, is used to write double consonants such as tt, kk, pp and ss. The consonant that follows っ is held for one extra beat, so the sound of a pause appears in the word. A short pause changes the word: かった (katta, won) and かた (kata, shoulder) are different words.

explanations.title: A double n
explanations.body: A double n, as in さんねん (sannen, three years), is written with ん plus a kana that begins with an n sound (な, に, ぬ, ね or の). The ん counts as its own beat.

lessons.title: 7. Long vowels, ん, dropped vowels and accent
lessons.subtitle: おばさん と おばあさん · ee と oo · ん の おと · ピッチ

explanations.title: Long vowels
explanations.body: When the same vowel is written twice in a row, the vowel is pronounced about twice as long as a single one. Hold it long enough, because the length changes the word.

explanations.title: The long ee and oo
explanations.body: The long ee is usually written by adding い to an e-column kana (せいかつ). In a few words, え is used instead (えいが is written with い, but おねえさん uses え). The long oo is in most cases written by adding う to an o-column kana, but a few words use お for historical reasons.

explanations.title: Words that differ by vowel length
The sound of ん
explanations.body: ん has the length of a full syllable, but its sound depends on what follows it. Japanese speakers are not normally aware of the differences, so you need not worry about them. Before n, t, d, s and z it is “n”, as in おんな (onna, woman). Before m, p and b it is “m”, as in さんぽ (sampo, stroll). Before k and g it is “ng” as in “song”, as in まんが (manga, comics). Before a vowel or at the end of a word it nasalizes the vowel before it, as in ほん (book) and れんあい (romance).

explanations.title: Vowels that are dropped
explanations.body: The vowels i and u are sometimes dropped when they stand between voiceless consonants (k, s, t, p and h), or at the end of an utterance after one. For example, すきです sounds like “s(u)kides(u)”.

examples.text: すきです。
examples.translation: Suki desu. — (I) like it.

explanations.title: Accent
explanations.body: Japanese has pitch accent. Every syllable is pronounced at about the same length and stress, and is either high or low in pitch. English stress accent, by contrast, makes syllables longer and louder. Pitch patterns vary a lot by region. This course does not mark accent; do not worry about it, and imitate the audio you hear. For example: あさ (morning), なまえ (name) and たかい (high; expensive) are pronounced with different pitch patterns.

explanations.title: Choose the correct hiragana
explanations.body: The book’s Practice A: pick the right kana of a look-alike pair for the romaji. The answers: yo よ (not ま), ho ほ (not は), me め (not ぬ), su す (not む), ki き (not さ), chi ち (not さ), ta た (not に), ro ろ (not る), e え (not ん). Look-alike pairs are the heart of learning kana: ぬ/め, は/ほ, さ/き/ち, る/ろ, ま/よ.

lessons.title: 9. Katakana: the forty-six basic characters
lessons.subtitle: ア イ ウ エ オ · カ · サ · タ · ナ · ハ · マ · ヤ · ラ · ワ ヲ · ン

explanations.title: Same sounds, different shapes
explanations.body: Katakana stand for the same forty-six sounds as hiragana, written with straighter lines. They are used mainly for loanwords and foreign names. Tap a character to hear it.

tables.title: Katakana basic syllables: romaji
tables.note: シ, チ, ツ and フ are romanized shi, chi, tsu and fu, like their hiragana counterparts. ヲ is pronounced o and is rarely used. ン is written n.

explanations.title: Look-alikes
explanations.body: Some pairs are easy to mix up when you start: シ (shi) and ツ (tsu), ソ (so) and ン (n), ク (ku) and ワ (wa), ヌ (nu) and ス (su), メ (me) and ヌ (nu), ナ (na) and メ (me). Notice the direction of the strokes: シ and ツ lean differently.

rows: シ: strokes lean sideways; ツ: strokes point downward
ソ: top stroke is short and steep; ン: dots lie flatter
ワ has a vertical stroke on the left

explanations.body: The dakuten (゛) and handakuten (゜) are added to the same rows, and contracted sounds use a small ャ, ュ or ョ after an i-column character. The pronunciation of katakana and its combinations is the same as that of the hiragana.

explanations.title: The long-vowel mark ー
explanations.body: In katakana, long vowels are written with a dash (ー). When writing vertically, the mark is written vertically too. Hold the vowel for two beats.

explanations.body: Katakana adds combinations with a small vowel letter to write foreign sounds that did not exist in Japanese.

explanations.title: The sound “v”
explanations.body: The sound “v” is sometimes written with ヴ. For example, “Venus” is written ビーナス or ヴィーナス.

lessons.title: 12. Kanji: what they are and how they work
lessons.subtitle: 音読み と 訓読み · Four kinds of kanji · Joyo kanji

explanations.title: What kanji are
explanations.body: Kanji are Chinese characters, introduced to Japan more than 1,500 years ago, when the Japanese language did not yet have a writing system. Hiragana and katakana developed later in Japan from simplified Chinese characters. Kanji represent both meanings and sounds.

explanations.title: Two kinds of readings
explanations.body: Most kanji have more than one reading. There are two kinds: on-yomi (Chinese readings) come from the pronunciation used in China at the time; some kanji have several on-yomi because of changes over time and across regions. Kun-yomi (Japanese readings) were added when people began to use kanji to write native Japanese words.

explanations.title: How many kanji
explanations.body: By the time of high school graduation, Japanese are expected to know 2,136 kanji, called the Joyo kanji, which the Ministry of Education designates as commonly used. 1,006 are taught at the elementary school level, and most of the rest in junior high school.

explanations.title: Four kinds of kanji by how they are formed
explanations.body: Roughly four types, by formation:

rows: dots and lines for numbers or abstract ideas
日 (sun) + 月 (moon) → 明 (bright); 人 (person) + 木 (tree) → 休 (to rest)
a meaning element and a sound element
氵 (water) + 青 (sei) → 清 (sei, clean); 日 (sun) + 青 (sei) → 晴 (sei, clear sky)

explanations.title: Name tags: your name in katakana
explanations.body: Foreign names are normally written in katakana in their own order (first name, then surname), with a dot ・ or a space between them: Mary Hart → メアリー・ハート. Japanese names place the family name first: たなか たけし. East Asian names such as Korean or Chinese names can be written in kanji: Yao Ming → ヨウ メイ or 姚明.

explanations.title: Reading practice: things Mary owns
explanations.body: Mary wrote about four things (a hat, a bicycle, a dictionary and shoes). The sentences use what you will learn in Lesson 2 (これ, の, じゃないです); the translations are mine.

examples.text: これは わたしの ぼうしじゃないです。 キャシーさんの ぼうしです。 ニューヨークヤンキースの ぼうしです。
examples.translation: Kore wa watashi no booshi janai desu. Kyashii-san no booshi desu. Nyuuyookuyankiisu no booshi desu. — This is not my hat. It is Cathy’s hat. It is a New York Yankees hat.

examples.text: これは わたしの じてんしゃです。 オーストラリアの じてんしゃです。 たかいです。
examples.translation: Kore wa watashi no jitensha desu. Oosutoraria no jitensha desu. Takai desu. — This is my bicycle. It is an Australian bicycle. It is expensive.

examples.text: これは ミシェルさんの じしょです。 スペインごの じしょじゃないです。 フランスごの じしょです。
examples.translation: Kore wa Misheru-san no jisho desu. Supeingo no jisho janai desu. Furansugo no jisho desu. — This is Michelle’s dictionary. It is not a Spanish dictionary. It is a French dictionary.

examples.text: これは ジャクソンさんの くつです。 イタリアの くつじゃないです。 アメリカの くつです。
examples.translation: Kore wa Jakuson-san no kutsu desu. Itaria no kutsu janai desu. Amerika no kutsu desu. — These are Jackson’s shoes. They are not Italian shoes. They are American shoes.

lessons.title: 15. Expression notes on greetings
lessons.subtitle: おはよう / ありがとう · さようなら · すみません · いいえ · family greetings

explanations.title: おはよう, ありがとう: short and long forms
explanations.body: おはよう is used between friends and family members, while おはよう ございます is used between less intimate acquaintances; the same goes for ありがとう and ありがとう ございます. The rule of thumb: if you are on a first-name basis with someone, go for the shorter versions. If you would address someone as Mr. or Ms., use the longer versions.

examples.text: おはよう。
examples.translation: Ohayoo. — Good morning. (friends, family)

examples.text: おはよう ございます。
examples.translation: Ohayoo gozaimasu. — Good morning. (people you call Mr./Ms.)

explanations.title: おはよう is for the morning
explanations.body: おはよう is the greeting used before noon, but some people use it in casual settings in the afternoon, or even at night, when they see their classmates or co-workers for the first time that day.

explanations.title: さようなら
explanations.body: There are several good-bye expressions in Japanese, and the choice depends on the degree of separation. さようなら indicates that the speaker does not expect to see the person spoken to before she “turns a page in her life”: not until a new day arrives, or until fate brings the two together again. It sounds dramatic and ritualistic, and its daily use is largely restricted to school children taking leave of their teachers.

rows: See you.; See you later. (between friends)
Excuse me. (taking leave, e.g. from a professor’s office)

explanations.title: すみません: three meanings
explanations.body: すみません means (1) “Excuse me,” to get another person’s attention, (2) “I’m sorry,” to apologize for the trouble you have caused, or (3) “Thank you,” to show appreciation for what someone has done for you.

examples.text: すみません。
examples.translation: Sumimasen. — Excuse me. / I’m sorry. / Thank you.

explanations.title: いいえ
explanations.body: いいえ is primarily “No,” a negative reply to a question. In the dialogue it is used to express the English phrase “Don’t mention it” or “You’re welcome,” with which you point out that one is not required to feel obliged for what you have done for them.

examples.text: いいえ。
examples.translation: Iie. — No. / Don’t mention it.

explanations.title: いってきます, いってらっしゃい, ただいま, おかえりなさい
explanations.body: いってきます and いってらっしゃい are a common exchange used at home when a family member leaves. The person who leaves says いってきます, literally “I will go and come back.” The family members answer いってらっしゃい, “Please go and come back.” ただいま and おかえり are used when a person comes home. The person who arrives says ただいま (“I am home right now”) to the family members, and they respond with おかえりなさい (“Welcome home”).

examples.translation: Leaving: Ittekimasu. — I’m off.

examples.translation: Family: Itterasshai. — See you later.

examples.text: ただいま。
examples.translation: Arriving: Tadaima. — I’m home.

examples.text: おかえりなさい。
examples.translation: Family: Okaerinasai. — Welcome home.

explanations.title: Practice: what do you say?
explanations.body: The book asks you to act these situations out with classmates. Here is a model answer for each (the book gives none, so these are mine).

rows: You meet your host family for the first time. Greet them.
はじめまして。 よろしく おねがいします。
It is one o’clock in the afternoon. You see your neighbor Mr. Yamada.
You come to class in the morning. Greet your teacher. Greet your friends.

explanations.title: Culture note: greetings and bowing
explanations.body:
Japanese people greet each other by bowing, which has many other functions, such as expressing respect, gratitude, or apologies. There are different ways of bowing, ranging from a small nod of the head to a 45-degree bend at the waist. Generally, the longer and the deeper you bow, the more formal and respectful it appears to others.

Many Japanese tend to feel uncomfortable with physical contact, although handshaking is becoming quite common in business situations, especially those involving foreigners.

When meeting someone in a business situation for the first time, it is customary to exchange meishi (business cards) with a small bow. Etiquette guides list a vast number of rules and pointers, but just remember that the important thing is to clearly show your respect when exchanging meishi.

explanations.title: Dialogue 1: asking the time
explanations.body: Mary, an international student who just arrived in Japan, talks to a Japanese student, Takeshi. Tap a line to hear it.

examples.text: すみません。いま なんじですか。
examples.translation: メアリー: Sumimasen. Ima nanji desu ka. — Excuse me. What time is it now?

examples.text: じゅうにじはんです。
examples.translation: たけし: Juuniji han desu. — It’s half past twelve.

examples.text: ありがとう ございます。
examples.translation: メアリー: Arigatoo gozaimasu. — Thank you.

examples.text: いいえ。
examples.translation: たけし: Iie. — You’re welcome.

examples.text: あの、りゅうがくせいですか。
examples.translation: たけし: Ano, ryuugakusee desu ka. — Um… are you an international student?

examples.text: ええ、アリゾナだいがくの がくせいです。
examples.translation: メアリー: Ee, Arizona daigaku no gakusee desu. — Yes, I am a student at the University of Arizona.

examples.text: そうですか。せんこうは なんですか。
examples.translation: たけし: Soo desu ka. Senkoo wa nan desu ka. — I see. What is your major?

examples.text: にほんごです。いま にねんせいです。
examples.translation: メアリー: Nihongo desu. Ima ninensee desu. — Japanese. I am a sophomore now.

explanations.title: What to notice
explanations.body: Neither speaker says “I” or “you”: the Japanese leaves out what is clear from the situation. Sentences end with です, and a question is made by adding か. Mary and Takeshi use ありがとう ございます and いいえ, the polite and the “you’re welcome” forms from the Greetings unit.

lessons.title: 19. Numbers, time and age
lessons.subtitle: ゼロ いち に さん … ひゃく · いちじ にじ … · ふん · さい

explanations.title: Numbers
explanations.body: Numbers from zero to one hundred. Above ten, the tens and the ones are put side by side: じゅう (10) + いち (1) = じゅういち (11); に (2) + じゅう (10) = にじゅう (20); にじゅうさん is 23.

explanations.title: Other readings
explanations.body: Some numbers have a second reading. 0 is ゼロ or れい. 4 is usually よん, but し and よ appear in some combinations (よじ, four o’clock; よねんせい, fourth-year student). 7 is なな, but しち in しちじ (seven o’clock). 9 is きゅう, but く in くじ (nine o’clock).

rows: じゅうなな、じゅうしち
じゅうきゅう、じゅうく

explanations.title: Expression Note: numbers with changing sounds
explanations.body: Many number words have more than one pronunciation. For example: 1 is いち, but いっ in いっぷん (one minute) and いっさい (one year old). 2 is に, but when reading digits one by one (as in a phone number) it may be pronounced with a long vowel, にい. 3 is さん; the part after it may change shape, as in さんぷん, not さんふん. 4 is よん, but よねんせい and よじ; in some later combinations it is し (しがつ, April), and the part after it may change, as in よんぷん. 5 is ご; read out separately, it may be pronounced ごう. 6 is ろく, but ろっ in ろっぷん. 7 is なな, but しちじ for seven o’clock. 8 is はち, but usually はっ in はっぷん and はっさい. 9 is きゅう, but くじ for nine o’clock. 10 is じゅう, but じゅっ or じっ in じゅっぷん/じっぷん and じゅっさい/じっさい.

explanations.title: Time: hours
explanations.body: Add じ to the number. ごぜん (A.M.) and ごご (P.M.) go in front of the hour, and はん (half) goes after it.

examples.text: いま ごぜん くじです。
examples.translation: Ima gozen kuji desu. — It is nine in the morning now.

examples.text: いま ごご さんじはんです。
examples.translation: Ima gogo sanji han desu. — It is half past three in the afternoon now.

explanations.title: Time: minutes
explanations.body: Minutes use ふん or ぷん after the number, with some sound changes. The numbers 1, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 10 take ぷん (with small っ for 1, 6, 8 and 10); the others take ふん. For minutes 11–19 and for 20 and 30, the same endings follow the tens.

rows: じゅうはっぷん、じゅうはちふん
にじゅっぷん、にじっぷん
さんじゅっぷん、さんじっぷん

explanations.title: Age
explanations.body: Add さい after the number for “…years old.” The question is なんさい (How old are you?); おいくつ is a more polite way to ask. 20 years old is はたち, though にじゅっさい or にじっさい can also be used.

examples.text: なんさいですか。
examples.translation: Nansai desu ka. — How old are you?

examples.text: おいくつですか。
examples.translation: Oikutsu desu ka. — How old are you? (polite)

lessons.title: 20. Grammar 1: X は Y です and questions with か
lessons.subtitle: わたしは がくせいです · りゅうがくせいですか · なん, なんじ, なんさい, なんねんせい

explanations.title: です: “It is …”
explanations.body: “It is 12:30.” “I am a student.” “My major is the Japanese language.” All of these are expressed with a noun and the word です. Note that none of these sentences has a “subject” like the “it,” “I” and “my major” of the English versions. Sentences without subjects are very common in Japanese; speakers tend to omit the subject whenever they think it is clear to the listener what or who they are referring to.

examples.text: じゅうにじはんです。
examples.translation: Juuniji han desu. — (It) is half past twelve.

examples.text: がくせいです。
examples.translation: Gakusee desu. — (I) am a student.

examples.text: にほんごです。
examples.translation: Nihongo desu. — (My major) is the Japanese language.

explanations.title: XはYです
explanations.body: When it is not clear what is being talked about, we can say X は …, where X stands for the thing that is talked about, the “topic.” The pattern X は Y です identifies a person or a thing X as item Y: “X is Y. As for X, it is Y.” は is a particle: it attaches to a phrase and shows how it relates to the rest of the sentence. It is written は but pronounced wa.

examples.text: せんこうは にほんごです。
examples.translation: Senkoo wa nihongo desu. — (My) major is the Japanese language.

examples.text: わたしは スー・キムです。
examples.translation: Watashi wa Suu Kimu desu. — I am Sue Kim.

examples.text: やましたさんは せんせいです。
examples.translation: Yamashita-san wa sensee desu. — Mr. Yamashita is a teacher.

examples.text: メアリーさんは アメリカじんです。
examples.translation: Mearii-san wa amerikajin desu. — Mary is an American.

explanations.title: No “a” and no plural
explanations.body: Nouns like がくせい and せんせい stand alone, unlike the English “student” and “teacher,” which are preceded by “a.” Japanese has no item that corresponds to “a,” nor to the plural “-s.” Without background, a sentence like がくせいです is ambiguous: it may mean “We are / you are / they are students” as well as “I am / you are / she is a student.”

explanations.title: Questions: add か
explanations.body: It is very easy to form questions in Japanese: add か at the end of a statement. It is not customary to write a question mark at the end of a question sentence in Japanese. This is a “yes/no” question:

examples.text: りゅうがくせいです。
examples.translation: Ryuugakusee desu. — (I am) an international student.

examples.text: りゅうがくせいですか。
examples.translation: Ryuugakusee desu ka. — (Are you) an international student?

explanations.title: Question words
explanations.body: Question sentences can contain a question word like なん (what). In this lesson you learn: なんじ (what time), なんさい (how old), なんねんせい (what year in school). The question word for “what” has two pronunciations: なん is used immediately before です or before a counter like じ (o’clock); なに is used before a particle, and also in the word なにじん (person of what nationality).

examples.text: せんこうは なんですか。
examples.translation: Senkoo wa nan desu ka. — What is your major?

examples.text: せんこうは えいごです。
examples.translation: Senkoo wa eego desu. — (My major) is English.

examples.text: いま なんじですか。
examples.translation: Ima nanji desu ka. — What time is it now?

examples.text: いま くじです。
examples.translation: Ima kuji desu. — It is nine o’clock.

examples.text: メアリーさんは なんさいですか。
examples.translation: Mearii-san wa nansai desu ka. — How old are you, Mary?

examples.text: じゅうきゅうさいです。
examples.translation: Juukyuusai desu. — I’m nineteen years old.

examples.text: なんねんせいですか。
examples.translation: Nannensee desu ka. — What year are you in college?

examples.text: にほんじんですか。
examples.translation: Nihonjin desu ka. — Are you Japanese?

explanations.title: Telephone numbers
explanations.body: A telephone number is asked with でんわばんごうは なんですか and answered with the digits read one at a time, with の between the exchange and the last digits.

examples.text: でんわばんごうは なんですか。
examples.translation: Denwa bangoo wa nan desu ka. — What is your telephone number?

examples.text: いち はち ろくの なな さん よん さんです。
examples.translation: Ichi hachi roku no nana san yon san desu. — It is 186-7343.

lessons.title: 21. Grammar 2: noun の noun, names, and expression notes
lessons.subtitle: たけしさんの でんわばんごう · だいがくの せんせい · にほんの だいがく · あの · はい / ええ · さん

explanations.title: noun の noun
explanations.body: の is a particle that connects two nouns. The phrase さくらだいがくの がくせい means “a student at Sakura University.” The second noun, がくせい, provides the main idea (being a student), and the first, さくらだいがく, makes it more specific (not a high school but a college student). の is very versatile: in the first example below it acts like the English possessive (’s), but that is not the only role it can play.

examples.text: たけしさんの でんわばんごう
examples.translation: Takeshi-san no denwa bangoo — Takeshi’s phone number

examples.text: だいがくの せんせい
examples.translation: Daigaku no sensee — a college professor

examples.text: にほんごの がくせい
examples.translation: Nihongo no gakusee — a student of the Japanese language

examples.text: にほんの だいがく
examples.translation: Nihon no daigaku — a college in Japan

explanations.title: Word order: main idea last
explanations.body: In the first two examples the English and Japanese words are arranged in the same order; in the last two they are in the opposite order. Japanese is more consistent: the main idea always comes at the end, with any further description placed before it. A phrase of the form “noun の noun” acts more or less like one big noun. You can put it wherever you can put a noun:

examples.text: たけしさんの おかあさんは こうこうの せんせいです。
examples.translation: Takeshi-san no okaasan wa kookoo no sensee desu. — Takeshi’s mother is a high school teacher.

explanations.title: Culture note: Japanese names
explanations.body: When Japanese give their name, they say their family name first and their given name last (middle names do not exist). When introducing themselves they often say only their family name. Most Japanese names are written in kanji. For example, たなか is usually written 田中, which means “middle of the rice field.” Family names are often related to nature or geographical features. Because many kanji share the same reading, names with the same pronunciation may be written with different kanji; ゆうこ can be written 優子 or with other characters.

explanations.title: あの
explanations.body: あの indicates that you have some reservations about saying what you are going to say next. You may be worried about interrupting something someone is currently doing, or about sounding rude by asking personal questions, for example.

examples.text: あの、りゅうがくせいですか。
examples.translation: Ano, ryuugakusee desu ka. — Um… are you an international student?

explanations.title: はい / ええ
explanations.body: Both はい and ええ mean “yes” in response to yes-no questions. Compared to はい, ええ is more conversational and relaxed. In more informal situations, うん is used. はい is also used to respond to a knock at the door or to the calling of one’s name, meaning “Here.” (ええ cannot be used in that case.)

examples.text: はい。
examples.translation: Hai. — Yes. / Here.

examples.text: ええ、そうです。
examples.translation: Ee, soo desu. — Yes, that’s right.

explanations.title: そうですか
explanations.body: そうですか acknowledges that you have understood what was just said: “Is that so?” or “I see.”

examples.text: そうですか。
examples.translation: Soo desu ka. — I see.

explanations.title: Pronunciation of は
explanations.body: The particle は is pronounced “wa,” not “ha.” It should be written with は. All other instances of “wa” are written with わ. There are a few exceptions, such as こんにちは (good afternoon) and こんばんは (good evening), which are usually written with は.

examples.text: わたしの でんわばんごうは さん なな の はち ろく ろく ななです。
examples.translation: Watashi no denwa bangoo wa san nana no hachi roku roku nana desu. — My telephone number is 37-8667.

explanations.title: Giving your telephone number
explanations.body: The particle の is usually placed between the local exchange code and the last four digits. So 012-345-6789 is ゼロ いち に、さん よん ご の ろく なな はち きゅう.

explanations.title: せんせい
explanations.body: The word せんせい is usually reserved for describing somebody else’s occupation. わたしは せんせいです makes sense, but may sound slightly arrogant, because せんせい actually means an “honorable master.” If you (or a member of your family) are a teacher and want to be really modest, you can use the word きょうし instead.

examples.text: きょうし
examples.translation: Kyooshi — teacher (modest)

explanations.title: さん
explanations.body: さん is placed after a name as a generic title. It goes both with a given name and a family name. Children are referred to as ちゃん (and boys in particular as くん) rather than さん. Professors and doctors are usually referred to with the title せんせい. さん and other title words are never used in reference to oneself.

examples.text: やましたさん
examples.translation: Yamashita-san — Mr./Ms. Yamashita

examples.text: ゆうこちゃん
examples.translation: Yuuko-chan — Yuuko (a girl)

examples.text: たけしくん
examples.translation: Takeshi-kun — Takeshi (a boy)

examples.text: やましたせんせい
examples.translation: Yamashita sensee — Professor Yamashita

explanations.title: Referring to the person you are talking to
explanations.body: The word for “you,” あなた, is not very commonly used in Japanese. Instead, we use the name and a title like さん and せんせい to refer to the person we are talking to. So “Ms. Hart, are you Swedish?” should be the first sentence below, not the second.

examples.text: ハートさんは スウェーデンじんですか。
examples.translation: Haato-san wa suweedenjin desu ka. — Ms. Hart, are you Swedish? (natural)

examples.text: ハートさん、あなたは スウェーデンじんですか。
examples.translation: Haato-san, anata wa suweedenjin desu ka. — Ms. Hart, are you Swedish? (unnatural: avoid あなた)

explanations.title: Dialogue 1: at a flea market
explanations.body: Mary goes to a flea market. Tap a line to hear it.

examples.text: すみません。これは いくらですか。
examples.translation: メアリー: Sumimasen. Kore wa ikura desu ka. — Excuse me. How much is this?

examples.text: それは さんぜんえんです。
examples.translation: みせのひと: Sore wa sanzen en desu. — That is 3,000 yen.

examples.text: たかいですね。じゃあ、あのとけいは いくらですか。
examples.translation: メアリー: Takai desu ne. Jaa, ano tokee wa ikura desu ka. — It’s expensive. Well then, how much is that watch?

examples.text: あれは さんぜんごひゃくえんです。
examples.translation: みせのひと: Are wa sanzengohyaku en desu. — That is 3,500 yen.

examples.text: そうですか。あれも たかいですね。
examples.translation: メアリー: Soo desu ka. Are mo takai desu ne. — I see. That is expensive, too.

examples.text: これは せんはっぴゃくえんですよ。
examples.translation: みせのひと: Kore wa senhappyaku en desu yo. — This is 1,800 yen.

examples.text: じゃあ、そのとけいを ください。
examples.translation: メアリー: Jaa, sono tokee o kudasai. — Then, I’ll take that watch.

explanations.title: Dialogue 2: a lost wallet
explanations.body: A man finds a wallet on the ground.

examples.text: これは だれの さいふですか。
examples.translation: しらないひと: Kore wa dare no saifu desu ka. — Whose wallet is this?

examples.translation: メアリー: Watashi no saifu desu. — It’s my wallet.

examples.text: ありがとう ございます。
examples.translation: メアリー: Arigatoo gozaimasu. — Thank you very much.

explanations.title: Dialogue 3: at a restaurant
explanations.body: After shopping, Mary goes to a restaurant.

examples.text: いらっしゃいませ。メニューを どうぞ。
examples.translation: ウエートレス: Irasshaimase. Menyuu o doozo. — Welcome. Here’s the menu.

examples.text: どうも。これは なんですか。
examples.translation: メアリー: Doomo. Kore wa nan desu ka. — Thank you. What is this?

examples.text: どれですか。ああ、とんかつです。
examples.translation: ウエートレス: Dore desu ka. Aa, tonkatsu desu. — Which one? Oh, it is tonkatsu (pork cutlet).

examples.text: とんかつ？ さかなですか。
examples.translation: メアリー: Tonkatsu? Sakana desu ka. — Tonkatsu? Is it fish?

examples.text: いいえ、さかなじゃないです。にくです。おいしいですよ。
examples.translation: ウエートレス: Iie, sakana janai desu. Niku desu. Oishii desu yo. — No, it is not fish. It is meat. It is delicious.

examples.text: じゃあ、これを おねがいします。
examples.translation: メアリー: Jaa, kore o onegaishimasu. — Then, I’ll have this.

examples.text: すみません。トイレは どこですか。
examples.translation: メアリー: Sumimasen. Toire wa doko desu ka. — Excuse me. Where is the restroom?

examples.text: あそこです。
examples.translation: ウエートレス: Asoko desu. — It is over there.

examples.text: ありがとう ございます。
examples.translation: メアリー: Arigatoo gozaimasu. — Thank you very much.

explanations.title: What to notice
explanations.body: ね at the end (たかいですね) asks for agreement, and よ (せんはっぴゃくえんですよ; おいしいですよ) tells the listener something they may not know. 〜を ください asks for something, and 〜を おねがいします is a slightly more polite request, often used when ordering food.

lessons.title: 26. Numbers up to 99,999, and yen
lessons.subtitle: ひゃく · せん · まん · えん · さんびゃく ろっぴゃく はっぴゃく · さんぜん はっせん

explanations.title: Hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands
explanations.body: The tens, hundreds and thousands work as in English: じゅう, ひゃく, せん. Japanese also has a unit for tens of thousands, まん, so 20,000 is にまん (2 × 10,000), not nijuusen. Large numbers are sums of smaller numbers.

explanations.title: Sound changes
explanations.body: The words for 300, 600, 800, 3,000 and 8,000 involve sound changes. Counters whose first sound is h, like ひゃく (hundred), generally change shape after 3, 6 and 8: さんびゃく, ろっぴゃく, はっぴゃく. Some counters that begin with s, like せん (thousand), change shape after 3 and 8: さんぜん, はっせん. A single 1 is not said before ひゃく and せん (ひゃく, せん), but it is said before まん: いちまん.

explanations.title: Putting numbers together
explanations.body: A complicated number is the sum of its parts. For example, 234,567 is 23 × 10,000 + 4 × 1,000 + 5 × 100 + 6 × 10 + 7.

explanations.title: Yen
explanations.body: えん is added after the number: ごひゃくえん is 500 yen, せんえん 1,000 yen, いちまんえん 10,000 yen.

explanations.title: Culture note: Japanese money
explanations.body:
Japan’s official currency is the yen, pronounced えん. The bills and coins currently in circulation are the following: the 10,000-yen bill (a portrait of Yukichi Fukuzawa, 1835–1901, a philosopher and the founder of Keio University), the 5,000-yen bill (Ichiyo Higuchi, 1872–1896, a writer and poet), the 2,000-yen bill (Shurei Gate, the second gate of Shuri Castle in Okinawa), the 1,000-yen bill (Hideyo Noguchi, 1876–1928, a bacteriologist who devoted himself to yellow fever research), and the 500-, 100- and 10-yen coins (and the smaller ones). All bills and coins are different sizes; the bills slightly descend in length from 10,000 yen to 1,000 yen.

Although credit cards are now widespread in Japan, some small shops and restaurants do not accept them, even in major cities. Consequently most people carry a certain amount of cash, and ATMs can be found almost everywhere. Pre-paid cards are available for use for public transportation and shopping. Personal checks are not used in Japan.

lessons.title: 27. Grammar 1: これ, それ, あれ, どれ and この, その, あの, どの
lessons.subtitle: これは いくらですか · このとけいは いくらですか · どれが あなたの ペンですか

explanations.title: これ, それ, あれ, どれ
explanations.body: What do we do when we want to talk about things whose names we do not know? We say “this thing,” “that one,” and so forth. In Japanese we use これ, それ and あれ. これ refers to a thing close to you, the speaker (“this thing here”). それ is something close to the person you are talking to (“that thing in front of you”). あれ is a thing neither close to the speaker nor to the listener (“that one over there”).

examples.text: これは いくらですか。
examples.translation: Kore wa ikura desu ka. — How much is this?

examples.text: それは さんぜんえんです。
examples.translation: Sore wa sanzen en desu. — That is 3,000 yen.

examples.text: あれは わたしの ペンです。
examples.translation: Are wa watashi no pen desu. — That one over there is my pen.

examples.text: これは わたしの ペンです。
examples.translation: Kore wa watashi no pen desu. — This is my pen.

examples.text: それは わたしの ペンです。
examples.translation: Sore wa watashi no pen desu. — That is my pen.

explanations.title: どれ: “which one”
explanations.body: どれ is the word for “which.” Question words like どれ and なに cannot be followed by the particle は. Instead you must use the particle が.

examples.text: どれですか。
examples.translation: Dore desu ka. — Which one is it (that you are talking about)?

examples.text: どれが あなたの ペンですか。
examples.translation: Dore ga anata no pen desu ka. — Which one is your pen?

explanations.title: この, その, あの, どの + noun
explanations.body: If you want to be slightly more specific than これ, それ and あれ, you can use この, その and あの together with a noun. The これ series must always stand alone, while the この series must always be followed by a noun. So if you know the item in your hand is a watch (とけい), instead of これは いくらですか you can say このとけいは いくらですか.

examples.text: このとけいは いくらですか。
examples.translation: Kono tokee wa ikura desu ka. — How much is this watch?

examples.text: そのとけいは さんぜんえんです。
examples.translation: Sono tokee wa sanzen en desu. — That watch is 3,000 yen.

examples.text: あのとけいは さんぜんごひゃくえんです。
examples.translation: Ano tokee wa sanzengohyaku en desu. — That watch over there is 3,500 yen.

examples.text: どのとけいが さんぜんごひゃくえんですか。
examples.translation: Dono tokee ga sanzengohyaku en desu ka. — Which watch is 3,500 yen?

explanations.title: Summary
explanations.body: Because どの is a question word like どれ, we cannot use は with it; we must use が.

exercises.explanation: それ is near the listener.

exercises.explanation: あれ is far from both.

exercises.explanation: The これ series stands alone.

lessons.title: 28. Grammar 2: ここ, だれの, も, じゃないです, ね and よ
lessons.subtitle: ゆうびんきょくは どこですか · だれの かばんですか · メアリーさんも · にくじゃないです

explanations.title: ここ, そこ, あそこ, どこ
explanations.body: We learn just one more ko-so-a-do set: ここ, そこ, あそこ and どこ are words for places. You can ask for directions with どこ; if you are close by, you can point toward the place and answer あそこです. Directions are covered in Lesson 4.

examples.text: すみません。ゆうびんきょくは どこですか。
examples.translation: Sumimasen. Yuubinkyoku wa doko desu ka. — Excuse me. Where is the post office?

examples.text: ゆうびんきょくは あそこです。
examples.translation: Yuubinkyoku wa asoko desu. — The post office is right over there.

explanations.title: だれの noun
explanations.body: In Lesson 1 we learned things like メアリーさんの でんわばんごう (Mary’s phone number). We now learn how to ask who something belongs to. The question word for “who” is だれ, and for “whose” we simply add the particle の.

examples.text: これは だれの かばんですか。
examples.translation: Kore wa dare no kaban desu ka. — Whose bag is this?

examples.text: それは スーさんの かばんです。
examples.translation: Sore wa Suu-san no kaban desu. — That is Sue’s bag.

explanations.title: noun も: “… too”
explanations.body: To say “Item A is this, and item B is this, too,” use も. も is a particle that indicates that that item, too, has the given property. Notice that it replaces は, and that it must directly follow the item, in this case みちこさん. (In English “too” can come after the sentence as a whole; in Japanese it cannot.) Pattern: A は X です。 B も X です。

examples.text: たけしさんは にほんじんです。
examples.translation: Takeshi-san wa nihonjin desu. — Takeshi is a Japanese person.

examples.text: みちこさんも にほんじんです。
examples.translation: Michiko-san mo nihonjin desu. — Michiko is Japanese, too.

explanations.title: A note about も
explanations.body: We cannot use も to describe a situation like this: our friend Pat has dual citizenship; Pat is Japanese, but she is also American. To describe the second half we cannot say パットも アメリカじんです, because that would mean Pat, in addition to somebody who has been mentioned, is American. Neither can we say パットは アメリカじんも です. (Japanese speakers would say パットは アメリカじんでも あります.)

explanations.title: noun じゃないです: negative
explanations.body: To negate a statement of the form X は Y です where Y is a noun, replace です with じゃないです.

examples.text: やまださんは がくせいじゃないです。
examples.translation: Yamada-san wa gakusee janai desu. — Mr. Yamada is not a student.

explanations.title: Other styles of negative sentences
explanations.body: There are several stylistic variants. じゃないです is very colloquial. The more formal replacement for ないです is ありません. じゃ is a contraction of では, which is more formal and more appropriate in the written language. So in addition to the above sentence, you also find the two below.

rows: (X は) Y じゃないです。
(X は) Y じゃありません。
(X は) Y ではありません。

examples.text: やまださんは がくせいじゃありません。
examples.translation: Yamada-san wa gakusee ja arimasen. — Mr. Yamada is not a student. (more conservative speech)

examples.text: やまださんは がくせいではありません。
examples.translation: Yamada-san wa gakusee de wa arimasen. — Mr. Yamada is not a student. (formal, for writing)

explanations.title: Not for adjectives
explanations.body: The two sentences あれも たかいですね and おいしいですよ in the dialogues end with です but cannot be negated by replacing です with じゃないです, because たかい and おいしい are not nouns. あれも たかいじゃないです and おいしいじゃないです are not grammatical. Instead one would say たかくないです and おいしくないです. We will learn the conjugation pattern of adjectives in Lesson 5.

explanations.title: ね and よ
explanations.body: Statements often end with the tags ね or よ, depending on the way the speaker views the interaction with the listener. If the speaker is seeking the listener’s confirmation or agreement, ね (“right?”) can be added. よ (“I tell you”) is added to a statement if the speaker wants to assure the listener of what has been said; with よ added, a statement becomes an authoritative decree.

examples.text: リーさんの せんこうは ぶんがくですね。
examples.translation: Rii-san no senkoo wa bungaku desu ne. — Ms. Lee, your major is literature, right?

examples.text: これは にくじゃないですね。
examples.translation: Kore wa niku janai desu ne. — This is not meat, is it?

examples.text: とんかつは さかなじゃないですよ。
examples.translation: Tonkatsu wa sakana janai desu yo. — Let me assure you: tonkatsu is not fish.

examples.text: スミスさんは イギリスじんですよ。
examples.translation: Sumisu-san wa igirisujin desu yo. — (In case you’re wondering) Mr. Smith is British.

lessons.title: 29. Expression notes and classroom expressions
lessons.subtitle: ください · おねがいします · どうぞ · useful classroom words and phrases

explanations.title: (〜を) ください
explanations.body: (… を) ください is “Please give me X.” You can use it to request (concrete) items in general.

examples.text: そのとけいを ください。
examples.translation: Sono tokee o kudasai. — Please give me that watch.

explanations.title: (〜を) おねがいします
explanations.body: (… を) おねがいします is also a request for item X. When used to ask for a concrete object, it sounds slightly more upscale than ください. It is heard often when ordering food at a restaurant (“I will have …”). It can also be used to ask for “abstract objects,” such as repairs, explanations and understanding.

examples.text: これを おねがいします。
examples.translation: Kore o onegaishimasu. — I’ll have this, please.

explanations.title: (〜を) どうぞ
explanations.body: (… を) どうぞ is used when an offer is made with respect to item X. In the dialogue, the restaurant attendant uses it when she is about to hand the menu to the customer. It may also be used when a person is waiting for you to come forth with item X; a telephone operator asking for your name would probably say おなまえを どうぞ. (お is a politeness marker, so おなまえ is “your honorable name”.)

examples.text: メニューを どうぞ。
examples.translation: Menyuu o doozo. — Here is the menu, please.

examples.text: おなまえを どうぞ。
examples.translation: Onamae o doozo. — Your name, please.

explanations.title: Practice: how much are they?

rows: ひゃくじゅうえんです。
せんごひゃくえんです。

examples.text: ペンは いくらですか。
examples.translation: Pen wa ikura desu ka. — How much is the pen?

examples.text: はちじゅうえんです。
examples.translation: Hachijuu en desu. — It is 80 yen.

explanations.title: Practice: what is that?
explanations.body: Practice II A: items (1)–(6) are near you and items (7)–(12) near your friend. Your friend asks what they are. Pay attention to これ and それ: use これ for things near you, それ for things near the other person.

examples.text: それは なんですか。
examples.translation: Friend: Sore wa nan desu ka. — What is that?

examples.text: これは ペンです。
examples.translation: You: Kore wa pen desu. — This is a pen.

examples.text: これは なんですか。
examples.translation: Friend: Kore wa nan desu ka. — What is this?

examples.text: それは ティーシャツです。
examples.translation: You: Sore wa tiishatsu desu. — That is a T-shirt.

explanations.title: Practice: what is that building?
explanations.body: Practice II B: the buildings in the picture are a library (the example), Sakura University, a bank, a post office and a coffee shop. The model answers (mine):

examples.text: あれは としょかんです。
examples.translation: Are wa toshokan desu. — That is the library.

examples.text: あれは さくらだいがくです。
examples.translation: Are wa Sakura daigaku desu. — That is Sakura University.

examples.text: あれは ぎんこうです。
examples.translation: Are wa ginkoo desu. — That is the bank.

examples.text: あれは ゆうびんきょくです。
examples.translation: Are wa yuubinkyoku desu. — That is the post office.

examples.text: あれは きっさてんです。
examples.translation: Are wa kissaten desu. — That is the coffee shop.

explanations.title: Practice: この, その, あの with prices
explanations.body: Practice III A: say how much the item is, using この (near you), その (near your partner) or あの (far from both). The example is このえんぴつは ろくじゅうえんです。

examples.text: このえんぴつは ろくじゅうえんです。
examples.translation: Kono enpitsu wa rokujuu en desu. — This pencil is 60 yen.

examples.text: あのコンピューターは ろくまん はっせんえんです。
examples.translation: Ano konpyuutaa wa rokuman hassen en desu. — That computer over there is 68,000 yen.

examples.text: あのじてんしゃは いちまん ななせんえんです。
examples.translation: Ano jitensha wa ichiman nanasen en desu. — That bicycle over there is 17,000 yen.

explanations.title: Practice: where is it?
explanations.body: Practice IV: look at the pictures and answer where each thing is. The example conversation:

rows: トイレは どこですか。
としょかんは どこですか。
くつは どこですか。
やましたせんせいは どこですか。
メニューは どこですか。
じしょは どこですか。

examples.text: すみません。ぎんこうは どこですか。
examples.translation: A: Sumimasen. Ginkoo wa doko desu ka. — Excuse me. Where is the bank?

examples.text: あそこです。
examples.translation: B: Asoko desu. — It is over there.

examples.text: ありがとう ございます。
examples.translation: A: Arigatoo gozaimasu. — Thank you.

explanations.body: Practice V asks about the belongings of Mary, Takeshi, Robert and Professor Yamashita (Picture A and B left out). The pattern: これは だれの かさですか → メアリーさんの かさです。 Practice VI: describe pictures with も.

explanations.title: The chart
explanations.body: Practice VII uses the chart from Lesson 1 (without the age row). Look at it, then answer the ten questions in the next card.

explanations.title: Questions and answers
explanations.body: Each question can be answered ええ、そうです。 when it is right. When it is wrong, say いいえ、…じゃないです。 and add the right information. The book gives one example (メアリーさんは にほんじんですか → いいえ、にほんじんじゃないです。アメリカじんです。); the answers to the ten questions are mine.

rows: たけしさんは ちゅうごくじんですか。
いいえ、ちゅうごくじんじゃないです。にほんじんです。
ロバートさんは アメリカじんですか。
いいえ、アメリカじんじゃないです。イギリスじんです。
やましたせんせいは かんこくじんですか。
いいえ、かんこくじんじゃないです。にほんじんです。
ロバートさんの せんこうは にほんごですか。
いいえ、にほんごじゃないです。ビジネスです。
スーさんの せんこうは けいざいですか。
いいえ、けいざいじゃないです。コンピューターです。
たけしさんは さくらだいがくの がくせいですか。
Is Takeshi a student at Sakura University?
メアリーさんは ロンドンだいがくの がくせいですか。
Is Mary a student at the University of London?
いいえ、ロンドンだいがくの がくせいじゃないです。アリゾナだいがくの がくせいです。
たけしさんは にねんせいですか。
いいえ、にねんせいじゃないです。よねんせいです。
スーさんは いちねんせいですか。
いいえ、いちねんせいじゃないです。さんねんせいです。
ロバートさんは よねんせいですか。

explanations.body: Mary and Takeshi are talking. From this lesson on the text is written with kanji, as in a real Japanese book; the romaji under each line shows how to read it. Tap a line to hear it.

examples.text: メアリーさん、週末はたいてい何をしますか。
examples.translation: たけし: Mearii-san, shuumatsu wa taitee nani o shimasu ka. — Mary, what do you usually do on the weekend?

examples.text: そうですね。たいていうちで勉強します。でも、ときどき映画を見ます。
examples.translation: メアリー: Soo desu ne. Taitee uchi de benkyoo shimasu. Demo, tokidoki eega o mimasu. — Let’s see. I usually study at home. But I sometimes see movies.

examples.text: そうですか・・・。じゃあ、土曜日に映画を見ませんか。
examples.translation: たけし: Soo desu ka... Jaa, doyoobi ni eega o mimasen ka. — I see… Then, would you like to see a movie on Saturday?

examples.text: 土曜日はちょっと・・・。
examples.translation: メアリー: Doyoobi wa chotto... — Saturday is not a good day. (lit., Saturday is a little bit [inconvenient]…)

examples.text: じゃあ、日曜日はどうですか。
examples.translation: たけし: Jaa, nichiyoobi wa doo desu ka. — Then, how about Sunday?

examples.text: いいですね。
examples.translation: メアリー: Ii desu ne. — That’s fine.

explanations.title: Dialogue 2: Sunday morning
explanations.body: On Sunday morning, at Mary’s host family’s.

examples.text: おはようございます。
examples.translation: メアリー: Ohayoo gozaimasu. — Good morning.

examples.text: おはよう。早いですね。
examples.translation: お母さん: Ohayoo. Hayai desu ne. — Good morning. You are early, aren’t you?

examples.text: ええ、今日は京都に行きます。京都で映画を見ます。
examples.translation: メアリー: Ee, kyoo wa Kyooto ni ikimasu. Kyooto de eega o mimasu. — Yes, I’m going to Kyoto today. I will see a movie in Kyoto.

examples.text: いいですね。何時ごろ帰りますか。
examples.translation: お母さん: Ii desu ne. Nanji goro kaerimasu ka. — Good. Around what time will you come back?

examples.text: 九時ごろです。
examples.translation: メアリー: Kuji goro desu. — Around nine.

examples.text: 晩ご飯は？
examples.translation: お母さん: Bangohan wa? — How about dinner?

examples.text: 食べません。
examples.translation: メアリー: Tabemasen. — I will not eat.

examples.text: そうですか。じゃあ、いってらっしゃい。
examples.translation: お母さん: Soo desu ka. Jaa, itterasshai. — I see. Well, have a nice day.

examples.text: いってきます。
examples.translation: メアリー: Ittekimasu. — Good-bye. (I’ll go and come back.)

explanations.title: What to notice
explanations.body: ませんか is used to invite someone (土曜日に映画を見ませんか), and ちょっと is a polite way to turn an invitation down: Japanese people don’t normally reject invitations with いいえ because it sounds too direct. 何時ごろ means “around what time”. 食べません is the negative of 食べます.

examples.text: 土曜日に映画を見ませんか。
examples.translation: Doyoobi ni eega o mimasen ka. — Would you like to see a movie on Saturday?

examples.text: 土曜日はちょっと・・・。
examples.translation: Doyoobi wa chotto... — Saturday is a bit (inconvenient).

lessons.title: 34. Grammar 1: verb forms: ます and ません
lessons.subtitle: 食べる → 食べます → 食べません · ru-verbs · u-verbs · する and くる

explanations.title: Verbs change shape
explanations.body: Verbs in Japanese conjugate, or take various shapes. In this lesson we learn three forms: (1) the “dictionary forms,” (2) the present tense affirmative forms, and (3) the present tense negative forms. There are two kinds of verbs that follow regular conjugation patterns, and two irregular verbs.

explanations.title: Ru-verbs
explanations.body: 食べる belongs to the group of verbs called “ru-verbs”: you add the suffix る to the verb base (tabe-) to form the dictionary form. For the two long forms of this lesson you simply add ます and ません instead of る. We learn four ru-verbs: 食べる, 寝る, 起きる, 見る.

explanations.title: U-verbs
explanations.body: The dictionary form of an u-verb like 行く can be broken down into the base (ik-) and the suffix u. The long forms (行きます, 行きません) are formed with the base plus imasu and imasen. In u-verb conjugations you find the letters shifting in the same row of the hiragana chart: in 行く you see く and き, both in the か row; 飲む has む and み, both in the ま row. We learn six u-verbs: 飲む, 読む, 話す, 聞く, 行く, 帰る.

explanations.title: Irregular verbs
explanations.body: There are two irregular verbs, する and くる, whose vowels differ between the dictionary (short) form and the long forms. The verb 勉強する, “to study,” conjugates just like する, because する is also used to form compound verbs.

explanations.title: Stems and memorizing
explanations.body: Later lessons refer to the part before ます and ません: for ru-verbs (the base: 食べ) and for u-verbs (the base plus i: 行き). We call these parts “stems.” For the irregular verbs the stems are し and き. It is a good idea to memorize each verb as a set: the dictionary form and the ます form together, such as 行く – 行きます. This is especially important with verbs that end in る, because they may be irregular verbs (する, くる), ru-verbs, or u-verbs whose bases just happen to end with r: knowing the class tells you why 帰ます and 帰ります are not the same: 帰る is a u-verb, so 帰ります is right and ×帰ます is wrong.

explanations.title: Telling ru-verbs from u-verbs ending in る
explanations.body: Look at the second from the last syllable of the dictionary form. If you see the vowels a, u or o right before the final る, you can be sure it is a u-verb. If you see i or e, in most cases it is a ru-verb (見る みる, 食べる たべる), but there are exceptions: 帰る かえる is a u-verb with an e before る.

rows: 帰ります / 帰りません

explanations.title: A note on other negative forms
explanations.body: In addition to the standard negatives like 食べません and 行きません, you may hear the much more colloquial negative forms like 食べないです and 行かないです. Lesson 8 returns to these. “Present tense” in Japanese means both the present and the future, as the next lesson shows.

lessons.title: 35. Grammar 2: the present tense and the particles を, で, に, へ
lessons.subtitle: コーヒーを飲みます · 図書館で本を読みます · 京都に行きます · 学校へ行きます

explanations.title: What “present tense” means
explanations.body: In this lesson we learn about a dozen verbs that describe basic human actions, often called “action verbs.” The “present tense” of these verbs means either (1) that a person habitually or regularly engages in these activities, or (2) that a person will, or is planning to, perform them in the future.

examples.text: 私はよくテレビを見ます。
examples.translation: Watashi wa yoku terebi o mimasu. — I often watch TV. (habitual)

examples.text: メアリーさんはときどき朝ご飯を食べません。
examples.translation: Mearii-san wa tokidoki asagohan o tabemasen. — Mary sometimes doesn’t eat breakfast. (habitual)

examples.text: 私は明日京都に行きます。
examples.translation: Watashi wa ashita Kyooto ni ikimasu. — I will go to Kyoto tomorrow. (future)

examples.text: スーさんは今日うちに帰りません。
examples.translation: Suu-san wa kyoo uchi ni kaerimasen. — Sue will not return home today. (future)

explanations.title: Particles
explanations.body: Nouns used in sentences generally must be followed by particles, which indicate the relations that the nouns bear to the verbs. (In spoken language particles are often “dropped”; Lesson 15 returns to this.) In this lesson we learn four: を, で, に and へ.

explanations.title: を: the direct object
explanations.body: The particle を indicates the “direct object,” the kind of thing that is directly involved in, or affected by, the event. Note that it is pronounced “o.”

examples.text: コーヒーを飲みます。
examples.translation: Koohii o nomimasu. — I drink coffee.

examples.text: 音楽を聞きます。
examples.translation: Ongaku o kikimasu. — I listen to music.

examples.text: テレビを見ます。
examples.translation: Terebi o mimasu. — I watch TV.

explanations.title: で: where the event takes place
explanations.body: The particle で indicates where the event described by the verb takes place. (Later lessons introduce verbs that require particles other than で to express location.)

examples.text: 図書館で本を読みます。
examples.translation: Toshokan de hon o yomimasu. — I will read books in the library.

examples.text: うちでテレビを見ます。
examples.translation: Uchi de terebi o mimasu. — I will watch TV at home.

explanations.title: に: goal of movement, and time
explanations.body: The particle に has many meanings; here we learn two: (1) the goal toward which things move, and (2) the time at which an event takes place.

examples.text: 私は今日学校に行きません。
examples.translation: Watashi wa kyoo gakkoo ni ikimasen. — I will not go to school today. (goal)

examples.text: 私はうちに帰ります。
examples.translation: Watashi wa uchi ni kaerimasu. — I will return home. (goal)

examples.text: 日曜日に京都に行きます。
examples.translation: Nichiyoobi ni Kyooto ni ikimasu. — I will go to Kyoto on Sunday. (time)

examples.text: 十一時に寝ます。
examples.translation: Juuichiji ni nemasu. — I will go to bed at eleven. (time)

explanations.title: ごろ: approximate time
explanations.body: Approximate time references are made by substituting ごろ, or ごろに, for に.

examples.text: 十一時ごろ寝ます。
examples.translation: Juuichiji goro nemasu. — I will go to bed at about eleven.

examples.text: 十一時ごろに寝ます。
examples.translation: Juuichiji goro ni nemasu. — I will go to bed at about eleven.

explanations.title: へ: goal of movement
explanations.body: The particle へ, too, indicates the goal of movement; the sentences above can be written with へ instead of に. Note that へ is pronounced “e.” へ may replace に only in the goal-of-movement sense: the に for time references and other uses cannot be replaced by へ.

examples.text: 私は今日学校へ行きません。
examples.translation: Watashi wa kyoo gakkoo e ikimasen. — I will not go to school today.

examples.text: 私はうちへ帰ります。
examples.translation: Watashi wa uchi e kaerimasu. — I will return home.

Which particle marks the direct object?
exercises.explanation: を marks what is acted on.

exercises.explanation: で marks the place of an action.

exercises.prompt: Which particle marks the goal of movement?
exercises.explanation: に and へ both mark the goal of movement.

exercises.prompt: Which particle marks a time?
exercises.explanation: へ cannot be used for time.

exercises.prompt: How is を pronounced?
How is へ pronounced as a particle?
Can へ replace に in 日曜日に行きます?
exercises.explanation: へ replaces に only for goals.

What does 私は明日京都に行きます mean?
options: I will go to Kyoto tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: What does 私はよくテレビを見ます mean?
How do you say “I will read books in the library”?

exercises.explanation: で marks the place; を marks the object.

lessons.title: 36. Grammar 3: time with に, ませんか, word order, adverbs and the topic は
lessons.subtitle: 日曜日に行きます · あした来ます · 食べませんか · よく · ときどき · あまり · ぜんぜん

explanations.title: Time references with に
explanations.body: You need the particle に with (1) days of the week, like “on Sunday,” and (2) numerical time expressions, like “at 10:45” or “in September.” (The sentences use the clock and months; the hours of the day are written with kanji.)

examples.text: 日曜日に行きます。
examples.translation: Nichiyoobi ni ikimasu. — I will go on Sunday.

examples.text: 十時四十五分に起きます。
examples.translation: Juuji yonjuugofun ni okimasu. — I get up at 10:45.

examples.text: 九月に帰ります。
examples.translation: Kugatsu ni kaerimasu. — I will go back in September.

explanations.title: No に after relative time words
explanations.body: You do not use に with (1) time expressions defined relative to the present moment, such as “today” and “tomorrow,” (2) expressions describing regular intervals, such as “every day,” and (3) the word for “when.”

examples.text: 明日来ます。
examples.translation: Ashita kimasu. — I will come tomorrow.

examples.text: 毎晩テレビを見ます。
examples.translation: Maiban terebi o mimasu. — I watch TV every evening.

examples.text: いつ行きますか。
examples.translation: Itsu ikimasu ka. — When will you go?

explanations.title: Parts of a day and the weekend
explanations.body: You normally do not use に with (1) the parts of a day, like “in the morning” and “at night,” and (2) the word for “weekend.” Unlike 明日 and 毎日, however, these words can be followed by に, depending on style, emphasis and personal preference.

examples.text: 朝、新聞を読みます。
examples.translation: Asa, shinbun o yomimasu. — I read the newspaper in the morning.

examples.text: 週末、何をしますか。
examples.translation: Shuumatsu, nani o shimasu ka. — What will you do on weekends?

explanations.title: ませんか: an invitation
explanations.body: You can use ませんか (the present tense negative plus the question particle) to extend an invitation. Its affirmative counterpart, ますか, cannot be used this way: a sentence like ご飯を食べますか can only be a question, not an invitation. To decline politely, say ちょっと… rather than いいえ.

examples.text: ご飯を食べませんか。
examples.translation: Gohan o tabemasen ka. — What do you say to having a meal with me?

examples.text: いいですね。
examples.translation: Ii desu ne. — Sounds great.

examples.text: テニスをしませんか。
examples.translation: Tenisu o shimasen ka. — Will you play tennis with me?

examples.text: うーん、ちょっと・・・。
examples.translation: Uun, chotto... — Um, it’s slightly (inconvenient for me at this moment).

explanations.title: Word order
explanations.body: Japanese sentences are fairly flexible in the arrangement of the elements. Generally, a sentence is made up of several noun-particle sequences followed by a verb or an adjective, which in turn is often followed by a sentence-final particle such as か, ね or よ. Among the noun-particle sequences, their relative order is to a large extent free. A typical sentence looks like the table below, but several other arrangements are possible.

examples.text: 私は今日図書館で日本語を勉強します。
examples.translation: Watashi wa kyoo toshokan de nihongo o benkyoo shimasu. — I will study Japanese in the library today.

examples.text: 私はよく七時ごろ、うちへ帰ります。
examples.translation: Watashi wa yoku shichiji goro, uchi e kaerimasu. — I often go back home at around seven.

explanations.title: Frequency adverbs
explanations.body: You can add a frequency adverb such as 毎日 (every day), よく (often) and ときどき (sometimes) to describe how often you do something. We also learn two adverbs which describe how infrequent something is: ぜんぜん (never; not at all) and あまり (not often; not very much). These adverbs anticipate the negative at the end of the sentence: if you use ぜんぜん or あまり you need to conclude the sentence with ません.

examples.text: 私はときどき喫茶店に行きます。
examples.translation: Watashi wa tokidoki kissaten ni ikimasu. — I sometimes go to a coffee shop.

examples.text: 私はぜんぜんテレビを見ません。
examples.translation: Watashi wa zenzen terebi o mimasen. — I do not watch TV at all.

examples.text: たけしさんはあまり勉強しません。
examples.translation: Takeshi-san wa amari benkyoo shimasen. — Takeshi does not study much.

explanations.title: The topic particle は
explanations.body: As we saw in Lesson 1, the particle は presents the topic of one’s utterance (“As for item X, it is such that …”). It puts forward the item you want to talk about and comment on. A topic phrase need not be the subject of a sentence: in the dialogue, non-subject phrases are made topics with は. “Let’s talk about weekends; what do you do on weekends?” and “Let me say what I will do today: I will go to Kyoto.”

examples.text: メアリーさん、週末はたいてい何をしますか。
examples.translation: Mearii-san, shuumatsu wa taitee nani o shimasu ka. — Mary, what do you usually do on the weekend?

examples.text: 今日は京都に行きます。
examples.translation: Kyoo wa Kyooto ni ikimasu. — I’m going to Kyoto today.

examples.text: 晩ご飯は？
examples.translation: Bangohan wa? — How about dinner?

examples.text: 食べません。
examples.translation: Tabemasen. — I will not eat.

explanations.title: は used to invite a comment
explanations.body: In 晩ご飯は？ the は directs the listener’s attention and invites a comment or the completion of the sentence. The topic 晩ご飯 does not stand in subject relation to the verb; it is its direct object.

exercises.explanation: Japanese rarely say いいえ to an invitation.

exercises.explanation: ぜんぜん needs ません.

exercises.explanation: あまり needs ません.

I sometimes go to a coffee shop.
I never go to a coffee shop.

exercises.prompt: Is the order of noun-particle sequences fixed?
exercises.explanation: Relative order is to a large extent free.

exercises.prompt: What comes at the end of a Japanese sentence?
options: the verb or adjective (then か, ね or よ)

exercises.prompt: In 晩ご飯は？ what does は do?
exercises.explanation: It directs attention to the topic.

lessons.title: 37. Expression notes and Japanese houses
lessons.subtitle: 行く / 来る · ちょっと · 日本の家

explanations.title: 行く / 来る
explanations.body: When you move to a place where the hearer is, you say “I’m coming” in English. In the same situation, 私は行きます is used in Japanese. 来る is a movement toward the place where the speaker is, while 行く is a movement in a direction away from the speaker.

examples.text: 私は行きます。
examples.translation: Watashi wa ikimasu. — I’m coming. (to where you are)

examples.text: あした、私のうちに来ませんか。
examples.translation: Ashita, watashi no uchi ni kimasen ka. — Won’t you come to my house tomorrow?

explanations.title: ちょっと
explanations.body: ちょっと literally means “a little,” “a bit,” “a small amount,” as in ちょっとください (Please give me a little) and ちょっと待ってください (Please wait for a moment). It is commonly used for a polite refusal. In that case it means “inconvenient,” “impossible,” and so on. Japanese people don’t normally reject requests, suggestions or invitations with いいえ (No), because it sounds too direct.

examples.text: 土曜日に映画を見ませんか。
examples.translation: A: Doyoobi ni eega o mimasen ka. — Will you see a movie on Saturday?

examples.text: 土曜日はちょっと・・・。
examples.translation: B: Doyoobi wa chotto... — Saturday is not convenient. (lit., Saturday is a little bit…)

explanations.title: Culture note: Japanese houses
explanations.body:
Traditionally, Japanese buildings were made of wood. Rooms were floored with tatami (rice-straw mats) and divided by fusuma or shooji (two types of sliding doors). Modern Japanese houses have mainly Western-style rooms, and are equipped with Western-style toilets. However, most bathrooms retain traditional characteristics: they are separated from toilets and sinks, and have some space for washing one’s body outside the bathtub. Usually all family members share the same bathtub water, so it is necessary to clean one’s body before getting into the bathtub.

Another traditional feature of Japanese homes is the genkan, a space inside the entrance where people remove their shoes.

rows: entrance area where shoes are taken off

exercises.prompt: What does 来る describe?
What does 行く describe?
options: movement away from the speaker’s place
exercises.explanation: 行く = away from the speaker.

exercises.prompt: In Japanese, what do you say when you go to where the listener is?
exercises.explanation: Where English says “I’m coming”, Japanese says 行きます.

exercises.prompt: What does ちょっと literally mean?
What can ちょっと mean when refusing?
exercises.explanation: ちょっと… = it isn’t convenient.

exercises.prompt: Why do people avoid いいえ when refusing an invitation?
exercises.explanation: Japanese people don’t normally reject invitations with いいえ.

exercises.prompt: What are tatami?
What are fusuma and shooji?
What is the genkan?
options: the entrance area where shoes are removed
exercises.explanation: Shoes come off in the genkan.

exercises.prompt: Is the bath usually separate from the toilet in a Japanese home?
exercises.explanation: Most bathrooms are separate from toilets and sinks.

exercises.prompt: What must you do before getting in the bath?
options: wash your body outside the tub
exercises.explanation: Family members share the bathwater, so wash first.

exercises.prompt: What is the ます form of のむ?

units.title: Genki I, Lesson 4: The First Date

lessons.title: 40. Dialogue: The First Date
lessons.subtitle: マクドナルドはどこですか · 映画はどうでしたか · きのう来ませんでしたね

explanations.title: Dialogue 1: Mary goes downtown
explanations.body: Mary asks a stranger for the way. Tap a line to hear it.

examples.text: すみません。マクドナルドはどこですか。
examples.translation: メアリー: Sumimasen. Makudonarudo wa doko desu ka. — Excuse me. Where is McDonald’s?

examples.text: あそこにデパートがありますね。マクドナルドはあのデパートの前ですよ。
examples.translation: 知らない人: Asoko ni depaato ga arimasu ne. Makudonarudo wa ano depaato no mae desu yo. — There is a department store over there. McDonald’s is in front of that department store.

examples.text: ありがとうございます。
examples.translation: メアリー: Arigatoo gozaimasu. — Thank you.

explanations.title: Dialogue 2: In the evening, at Mary’s host family’s house
explanations.body: Mary comes home and tells her host father about her day.

examples.text: ただいま。
examples.translation: メアリー: Tadaima. — I’m home.

examples.text: おかえりなさい。映画はどうでしたか。
examples.translation: お父さん: Okaerinasai. Eega wa doo deshita ka. — Welcome home. How was the movie?

examples.text: 見ませんでした。たけしさんは来ませんでした。
examples.translation: メアリー: Mimasen deshita. Takeshi-san wa kimasen deshita. — I didn’t see it. Takeshi didn’t come.

examples.text: えっ、どうしてですか。
examples.translation: お父さん: E, dooshite desu ka. — Oh, why?

examples.text: わかりません。だから、一人で本屋とお寺に行きました。
examples.translation: メアリー: Wakarimasen. Dakara, hitori de honya to otera ni ikimashita. — I don’t know. So, I went to a bookstore and a temple alone.

examples.text: 人がたくさんいましたか。
examples.translation: お父さん: Hito ga takusan imashita ka. — Were there a lot of people?

examples.text: はい。お寺で写真をたくさん撮りました。デパートにも行きました。はい、おみやげです。
examples.translation: メアリー: Hai. Otera de shashin o takusan torimashita. Depaato ni mo ikimashita. Hai, omiyage desu. — Yes. I took many pictures at the temple. I also went to a department store. Here’s a souvenir for you.

examples.text: ありがとう。
examples.translation: お父さん: Arigatoo. — Thank you.

explanations.title: Dialogue 3: Next day at school
explanations.body: Mary meets Takeshi, who had not appeared for the date.

examples.text: あっ、たけしさん。きのう来ませんでしたね。
examples.translation: メアリー: A, Takeshi-san. Kinoo kimasen deshita ne. — Oh, Takeshi. You didn’t come yesterday, did you?

examples.text: 行きましたよ。モスバーガーの前で一時間待ちました。
examples.translation: たけし: Ikimashita yo. Mosubaagaa no mae de ichijikan machimashita. — I did go there. I waited for one hour in front of the Mos Burger place.

examples.text: モスバーガーじゃないですよ。マクドナルドですよ。
examples.translation: メアリー: Mosubaagaa janai desu yo. Makudonarudo desu yo. — It’s not Mos Burger. It’s McDonald’s!

examples.text: マクドナルド・・・。ごめんなさい！
examples.translation: たけし: Makudonarudo... Gomennasai! — McDonald’s… I’m sorry!

explanations.title: What to notice
explanations.body: あります and います tell what exists and where (あそこにデパートがあります, 人がたくさんいました). Past tense is formed with ました and ませんでした (見ませんでした, 待ちました). どうして means “why” and だから means “so; therefore”. ごめんなさい is “I’m sorry” (apologizing for a mistake), while すみません is also used to get someone’s attention. Takeshi waited in front of the wrong restaurant: Mos Burger instead of McDonald’s.

examples.text: あそこにデパートがあります。
examples.translation: Asoko ni depaato ga arimasu. — There is a department store over there.

examples.text: だから、一人で本屋とお寺に行きました。
examples.translation: Dakara, hitori de honya to otera ni ikimashita. — So I went to a bookstore and a temple alone.

lessons.title: 42. Grammar 1: あります and います
lessons.subtitle: あそこにデパートがあります · 留学生がいます · 時間がありますか · テストがあります

explanations.title: Xがあります: “there is X”
explanations.body: Xがあります means “there is/are X (a nonliving thing)”. The particle が introduces, or presents, the item X. You can use あります when you want to say that there is something at a certain location.

examples.text: あそこにマクドナルドがあります。
examples.translation: Asoko ni Makudonarudo ga arimasu. — There’s a McDonald’s over there.

explanations.title: Three differences from other verbs
explanations.body: あります is different from the other verbs we have seen so far on three counts. (1) It calls for the particle に, rather than で, for the place description. (2) The place description usually comes at the beginning of the sentence. (3) The thing description is usually followed by the particle が, rather than は.

rows: で: 図書館で勉強します
に: 図書館に本があります

explanations.title: Having and events
explanations.body: You can also use あります to say that you have or own something, and to say that an event will take place (a test, a class, a party).

examples.text: テレビがありません。
examples.translation: Terebi ga arimasen. — I don’t have a TV.

examples.text: 時間がありますか。
examples.translation: Jikan ga arimasu ka. — Do you have time?

examples.text: 火曜日にテストがあります。
examples.translation: Kayoobi ni tesuto ga arimasu. — There will be an exam on Tuesday.

examples.text: あしたは日本語のクラスがありません。
examples.translation: Ashita wa nihongo no kurasu ga arimasen. — There will be no Japanese class tomorrow.

examples.text: あした京都でお祭りがあります。
examples.translation: Ashita Kyooto de omatsuri ga arimasu. — There will be a festival in Kyoto tomorrow.

explanations.title: Notes on あります
explanations.body: The colloquial negative of ある is ない: ないです (not the regular formation ×あらないです, which is ungrammatical). Note the difference between テレビがありません (“I don’t have a TV”, the negative of テレビがあります) and テレビじゃありません (“It isn’t a TV”, the negative of テレビです). When あります means that an event takes place, the place is followed by で as with normal verbs (京都でお祭りがあります), and the 時間 expressions follow the rule of Lesson 3: 日曜日に takes に, あした does not.

explanations.title: Xがいます: “there is X” (a person or animal)
explanations.body: When you want to present a person or some other sentient being, rather than a thing, you need to use the verb います. You can also use います to say that you have friends, siblings and so forth.

examples.text: あそこに留学生がいます。
examples.translation: Asoko ni ryuugakusee ga imasu. — There is an international student over there.

examples.text: 日本人の友だちがいます。
examples.translation: Nihonjin no tomodachi ga imasu. — I have a Japanese friend.

explanations.title: います and です
explanations.body: Note that the same English “is” comes out differently in Japanese. います and あります are strictly for descriptions of existence and location, while です is for description of an attribute of a person or a thing.

examples.text: そこに留学生がいます。
examples.translation: Soko ni ryuugakusee ga imasu. — There is an international student over there.

examples.text: メアリーさんは留学生です。
examples.translation: Mearii-san wa ryuugakusee desu. — Mary is an international student.

lessons.title: 43. Grammar 2: describing where things are
lessons.subtitle: XはYの前です · 上 · 下 · 中 · 右 · 左 · 近く · となり · 間

explanations.title: Asking where
explanations.body: We learned in Lesson 2 that to ask for the location of item X, you can use the word どこ (where) and say Xはどこですか. In response, one can of course point and say あそこ (over there), そこ (right there near you) or ここ (right here).

examples.text: マクドナルドはどこですか。
examples.translation: Makudonarudo wa doko desu ka. — Where’s McDonald’s?

examples.text: あそこです。
examples.translation: Asoko desu. — Over there.

explanations.title: Relative location: XはYの前です
explanations.body: In this lesson we learn to describe the location of an item relative to another item, as in “X is in front of Y”. The Japanese version looks like XはYの前です.

examples.text: マクドナルドはあのデパートの前です。
examples.translation: Makudonarudo wa ano depaato no mae desu. — McDonald’s is in front of that department store.

explanations.title: Location words
explanations.body: Other useful words describing locations are as follows. Each is placed after Yの, and between two things you use AとBの間.

rows: X is to the right of Y.
X is to the left of Y.
X is in front of Y.
X is between Y and Z.

examples.text: 銀行は図書館のとなりです。
examples.translation: Ginkoo wa toshokan no tonari desu. — The bank is next to the library.

examples.text: かさはテーブルの下です。
examples.translation: Kasa wa teeburu no shita desu. — The umbrella is under the table.

examples.text: レストランはデパートと病院の間です。
examples.translation: Resutoran wa depaato to byooin no aida desu. — The restaurant is between the department store and the hospital.

explanations.title: The picture in the book
explanations.body: The picture of the lesson shows each word with an example; the phrases written next to the objects are:

rows: 山田さんと佐藤さんの間
between Ms. Yamada and Mr. Sato

explanations.title: With action verbs
explanations.body: One can use any of the above location words together with a verb to describe an event that occurs in the place. To use these phrases with verbs such as 食べる and 待つ, you need the particle で.

examples.text: 私はモスバーガーの前でメアリーさんを待ちました。
examples.translation: Watashi wa Mosubaagaa no mae de Mearii-san o machimashita. — I waited for Mary in front of the Mos Burger place.

explanations.title: Notes
explanations.body: Another word for “near” that is also commonly used is そば. Both XはYのとなりです and XはYのよこです describe situations where two items (X and Y) are found side by side. For a となり sentence to be considered appropriate, items X and Y need to belong to the same category (two people, two buildings, and so forth). In contrast, an item can be よこ in relation to another item even if they are quite distinct.

examples.text: かばんはつくえのよこです。
examples.translation: Kaban wa tsukue no yoko desu. — The bag is by the desk.

examples.text: 山田さんのとなりは佐藤さんです。
examples.translation: Yamada-san no tonari wa Satoo-san desu. — Next to Ms. Yamada is Mr. Sato.

examples.text: マクドナルドはあのデパートの前です。
examples.translation: Makudonarudo wa ano depaato no mae desu. — McDonald’s is in front of that department store.

examples.text: 郵便局は駅の近くです。
examples.translation: Yuubinkyoku wa eki no chikaku desu. — The post office is near the station.

examples.text: 本はかばんの中です。
examples.translation: Hon wa kaban no naka desu. — The book is in the bag.

examples.text: 猫はいすの上です。
examples.translation: Neko wa isu no ue desu. — The cat is on the chair.

examples.text: ホテルは公園の右です。
examples.translation: Hoteru wa kooen no migi desu. — The hotel is to the right of the park.

examples.text: 病院は学校の左です。
examples.translation: Byooin wa gakkoo no hidari desu. — The hospital is to the left of the school.

examples.text: 図書館は大学の後ろです。
examples.translation: Toshokan wa daigaku no ushiro desu. — The library is behind the university.

explanations.title: Past tense of です
explanations.body: The past tense versions of “X は Y です” sentences look like the following.

explanations.title: More about the negative
explanations.body: As was the case with the present tense じゃないです, you also find a more conservative variant じゃありませんでした along with じゃなかったです. Written language would more likely have ではありませんでした, with the uncontracted form では.

explanations.title: Past tense of verbs
explanations.body: The past tense forms of verbs look like the following, where 〜 stands for the stem of a verb.

examples.translation: Watashi wa kinoo nihongo o benkyoo shimasen deshita. — I did not study Japanese yesterday.

explanations.title: Same rules as before
explanations.body: The various details of formation of the long forms that we learned in Lesson 3, like the ru-verb / u-verb / irregular verb distinctions, all apply to the past tense forms as well. The colloquial substandard form of the past tense negative of verbs is なかったです, as in 帰らなかったです; Lesson 8 shows how to change verbs into these forms.
